title: Genesis 48:8–22
context: Dim-eyed Israel blesses Joseph’s sons, crossing his hands so the right rests on Ephraim the younger. Joseph protests firstborn custom; Jacob refuses: “I know, my son, I know.” The blessing names God as shepherd and redeeming angel, sets Ephraim before Manasseh, and pledges return to the fathers’ land.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on Jacob’s crossed-hand blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh—so each camp speaks in its own voice on grace, birth order, and why the younger is set first.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Jacob gave him to understand that he knew what he did, and that he did it neither by mistake nor in a humour, nor from a partial affection to one more than the other, but from a spirit of prophecy. … God, in bestowing his blessings upon his people, gives more to some than to others. … Grace observes not the order of nature, nor doth God prefer those whom we think fittest to be preferred, but as it pleaseth him.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 48:16, 19)

arminian.quote: It is observable how God from the beginning has preferred the younger to the elder. … This is to be resolved entirely into the wise and secret counsel of God, so far as it regards temporal blessings and national privileges. … The grace that converts the soul certainly comes from the mere mercy of God, without any merit on man’s part; and a sufficiency of this is offered to every man. But it is not less certain that God loves those best who are most faithful to this grace.

reformed.quote: Moses says that he guided his hands wittingly, because he did not rashly put them forth. … Whence we gather that the Holy Spirit was the director of this act, who irradiated the mind of the holy man. … He errs in binding the grace of God to the accustomed order of nature: as if the Lord did not often purposely change the law of nature, to teach us that what he freely confers upon us is entirely the result of his own will.

Jacob does not dispute which of the youths shall be the more worthy; but only pronounces what God had decreed with himself, concerning each. … They are therefore altogether insane, who hew out dry and perforated cisterns, in seeking causes of divine adoption; whereas, everywhere, the Scripture defines in one word, that they are called to salvation whom God has chosen, and that the primary source of election is his free good pleasure.

verses.text: Israel saw Joseph’s sons, and said, “Who are these?”
verses.arminianNotes:
He sees yet asks, “Who are these?” Dim sight still wants names spoken.

Pastorally: recognition can be a question. Grace lets the father hear Joseph identify the boys before he blesses them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Israel “saw” and still inquired. The blessing will not be anonymous.

God often has His servants ask what they partly see. The question opens the rite.

verses.text: Joseph said to his father, “They are my sons, whom God has given me here.” He said, “Please bring them to me, and I will bless them.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Whom God has given me here”—Egypt’s gift named as God’s. Jacob asks them brought for blessing.

Classical Arminians love the confession. Children are received, not seized; the blessing is requested, not presumed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joseph traces the boys to God’s giving in this place. Jacob answers with a please and a purpose: bless them.

Fruit of the womb is gift. The patriarch will now spend what God deposited in him.

verses.text: Now the eyes of Israel were dim for age, so that he couldn’t see well. Joseph brought them near to him; and he kissed them, and embraced them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eyes dim; kiss and embrace still find them. Nearness heals what sight cannot.

Bodily weakness does not undo love. Joseph helps; Jacob holds. Means and affection work together.
verses.reformedNotes:
Blindness like Isaac’s—yet this time the hands will not be fooled.

Jacob’s eyes are dim, but his blessing is clear. God can guide crossed hands when sight fails.

verses.text: Israel said to Joseph, “I didn’t think I would see your face, and behold, God has let me see your offspring also.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He had not expected Joseph’s face; God has shown offspring too. Mercy outruns hope.

Grace often exceeds what we dared ask. The God who restored a son now shows grandsons.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Behold, God has let me see.” The unexpected is credited to God, not to luck or Egypt.

God has given Jacob more than he ever expected. The lost son and the double seed are the Lord’s showing.

verses.text: Joseph brought them out from between his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
From the knees, then Joseph bows to the earth. The vizier honors the dying shepherd.

Arminians see fitting reverence, not groveling for spectacle. A son’s bow is owed; the next act is the blessing he came for.
verses.reformedNotes:
The boys leave Jacob’s lap; Joseph’s face meets the ground.

Egypt’s lord becomes a worshiper at Israel’s bed. Rank yields to the prophet of the covenant.

verses.text: Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand, and brought them near to him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joseph arranges them for custom: Manasseh to Jacob’s right, Ephraim to the left. He wants the firstborn under the better hand.

The setup is sincere and almost right. Nature’s order is not wicked; it is about to be overruled.
verses.reformedNotes:
Positions are carefully set so the right hand will find Manasseh. Joseph catechizes by choreography.

Human arranging is not imaginary—and not final. The next verse will cross what Joseph lined up.

verses.text: Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it on Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands knowingly, for Manasseh was the firstborn.
verses.arminianNotes:
Right hand on the younger, hands crossed, firstborn named so we cannot miss it. Wesley: not mistake, humor, or partiality, but a spirit of prophecy.

Classical Arminians add Clarke’s caution: national and temporal preferments sit in God’s wise counsel; converting grace is still mercy offered with sufficiency to every man. The crossing is God’s pleasure, not a cartoon of a closed door.
verses.reformedNotes:
He guides his hands wittingly. Calvin: the Holy Spirit directed the act; Jacob was clearer-sighted in crossing arms than Joseph with open eyes.

God is not bound to primogeniture. What He freely confers is of His own will; the crossed hands preach that liberty.
verses.keyContrast: Both deny accident and petty favoritism. Arminians hear prophetic insight and God’s freedom in temporal gifts, while insisting converting grace is sincerely offered; Reformed readers hear the Spirit directing a sign of free election not bound to nature’s order.

verses.text: He blessed Joseph, and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day,
verses.arminianNotes:
The blessing of the boys is first a blessing of Joseph, and first a naming of God: walked-before, shepherd all my life.

A lifetime of being shepherded is testimony, not theory. Dying faith recites a God who can still be trusted for the lads.
verses.reformedNotes:
God of the fathers, shepherd of this man. The covenant Name is the fountain of the hands.

Jacob arrogates nothing. He blesses as a minister; the Shepherd is the source of the gift.

verses.text: the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads, and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac. Let them grow into a multitude upon the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The Angel who redeemed from all evil is asked to bless the boys. Clarke hears the Goel—Christ the redeeming Kinsman—invoked, not a mere creature.

Arminians pray this over children with confidence: the Redeemer who kept Jacob can keep them. Name and multitude are sought from Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the Angel is joined to God as equal—Christ the Mediator, already the bond between God and man.

Redemption from all evil is this Angel’s office. The name of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is laid on the boys because God Himself blesses.

verses.text: When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim, it displeased him. He held up his father’s hand, to remove it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s head.
verses.arminianNotes:
It displeased him; he takes the hand to move it. Love of the firstborn is understandable and still mistaken.

Good men can resist a strange mercy. Joseph is not mocked; he is corrected. Nature’s ranking is not the last word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joseph binds grace to birth order and tries to fix the rite. Calvin: he errs in chaining God’s gift to nature’s custom.

Even holy affection can fight election’s sign. The hand will not stay where flesh prefers.

verses.text: Joseph said to his father, “Not so, my father, for this is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Not so”—the firstborn argument, spoken with honor. Joseph catechizes his father in the usual rule.

Classical Arminians grant the rule’s ordinary justice. Jacob will not deny Manasseh’s greatness; he will deny that custom owns God’s right hand.
verses.reformedNotes:
Firstborn is Joseph’s axiom. He would put the right hand back on Manasseh.

The protest is filial and fleshly at once. God often teaches by refusing the axiom.

verses.text: His father refused, and said, “I know, my son, I know. He also will become a people, and he also will be great. However, his younger brother will be greater than he, and his offspring will become a multitude of nations.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“I know, my son, I know.” Manasseh will be a people and great; Ephraim greater still. Wesley: God often gives most to those least likely.

Clarke keeps the balance: temporal and national preferment may rest in secret counsel; that differs from saying converting grace is withheld from some by an arbitrary shut door. Both boys are blessed; the difference is degree of public greatness.
verses.reformedNotes:
He refuses. Calvin: Jacob does not weigh worth; he pronounces what God decreed. Dignity is hidden in God’s counsel until vocation makes it plain.

Seeking other cisterns for adoption’s cause is vain. The primary source of election is God’s free good pleasure—and Manasseh is still called great, so envy is forbidden.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear a true prophetic refusal, not a slip. Arminians typically keep Manasseh’s greatness and a sincere gospel offer in view while granting God’s freedom in public gifts; Reformed readers hear free election announced, causes of adoption located in God’s good pleasure alone.

verses.text: He blessed them that day, saying, “Israel will bless in your name, saying, ‘God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh’” He set Ephraim before Manasseh.
verses.arminianNotes:
The formula of later Israel: God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh. Both names stay in the blessing; Ephraim is put first.

The proverb is gift for the whole people. Preference is not legendary; exclusion of Manasseh is not.
verses.reformedNotes:
That day he sets the order: Ephraim before Manasseh. Israel will bless by their names.

The public proverb seals what the hands did. Grace toward both is conspicuous so the lesser will not envy.

verses.text: Israel said to Joseph, “Behold, I am dying, but God will be with you, and bring you again to the land of your fathers.
verses.arminianNotes:
I die; God will be with you and bring you home. Presence outlasts the dying father.

Classical Arminians rest here pastorally: the God who shepherded Jacob still invites the family to trust the road back. The promise is sincere for those who go with Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Death is named; God’s with-ness and the return are more certain than Jacob’s breath.

The covenant does not die with the patriarch. God will be with them and will bring them—the Lord who crossed the hands.

verses.text: Moreover I have given to you one portion above your brothers, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joseph is honored without the others being unnamed in later blessings.

Extra portions can be just; they need not become a gospel of favorites. The land gift points home, not to Egypt’s palaces.
verses.reformedNotes:
A slope taken from Amorites is laid on Joseph. John 4 will still know the parcel.

Even the extra lot is under promise. Jacob gives what faith already counts as his in the land of the fathers.
